title: The Mcf-separator: detecting and exploiting multi-commodity flow structures in MIPs
contribution: A separation heuristic for general MIPs, shipped in SCIP 1.2 and CPLEX 12.1, that detects embedded multi-commodity arc-flow networks in the constraint matrix and feeds network-cut aggregations to the solver's existing c-MIR routine, gated by a numeric inconsistency measure (pp. 2-3, 23-24).
problem_entry: A measured blind spot: c-MIR in SCIP/CPLEX rarely finds cut-based MIR network-design cuts because the network is unknown and the aggregation limit (7 rows in SCIP) is conservative; design constraint from Bixby and Rothberg: recognise the models it applies to, add little overhead elsewhere (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: All classical network-design cuts are MIR inequalities of one base inequality (6) from aggregating flow rows of S and capacity rows of δ−(S); so replace only the c-MIR aggregation (weights u, multipliers γ) and keep the solver's rounding machinery, with a consistency gate that switches cuts off when fit is poor (pp. 2-3, 7-9, 23-24).
assumptions: General MIP input; target arc-flow structure (2a)-(2d) plus multi-facility, unsplittable and undirected variants; detector relies on unscaled equal-magnitude flow rows, node degree <= 10% of arcs, similar-size commodities, near-complete coupling rows, and must survive presolve; validity needs nothing from the detector (pp. 2, 5, 12-28, 35).
proof_devices: base inequality (6), from which cutset, flow-cutset, dicut and flow-cover inequalities are derived as MIR inequalities (pp. 7-9)
validity invariant: every cut is an MIR inequality of an aggregation of original rows (p. 35)
Algorithms 1-4 detection pipeline: flow, arc, node detection and network construction by majority vote (pp. 14-20)
inconsistency ratios Ψ(a), Ψ(G) with thresholds 0.5 and 0.02 (pp. 11, 19)
Algorithm 5 separation with up to 20 multipliers and linear-time most-violated flow-cutset (pp. 23-25)
node-set selection by shrinking to 5 clusters with slack minus |dual| weights and connected shores (pp. 25-26)
experiments: SCIP 1.1.0.8 and CPLEX 12.1, 1 h limit, mcf vs nomcf from full default on 7 network-design sets, miplib, mittelmann and a 1266-model CPLEX-internal library; all/sep/nosep rows, easy/hard split, >=10 s and >=100 s subsets; time ratios 0.32-0.53 on target sets, 129/1388 affected with -17.9% time; detector checked against known networks; gate and cluster sensitivity studies; no seeds or time split (pp. 21-37).
positioning: Extends Marchand-Wolsey c-MIR, adapts Bixby-Fourer row-scanning network detection (no column scaling, commodity by commodity), borrows cut selection from network-design branch-and-cut; polyhedral facts cited not re-proved (pp. 2-3, 8, 10, 14-15, 23-26).
writing: Contribution in first sentence, each known inequality derived from (6) in a few lines, every constant printed with a pseudocode disclaimer, hedges next to small counts; abstract numbers looser than the body and companion report miscited as 07-38 (pp. 1-2, 7-9, 34-35, 39).
limits_future: cut.set and dense flow rows not detected, no gain on very easy sets, public general sets too small, 5 clusters gives up sndlib gain, flow covers not tried in SCIP; future: scan matrices for known structures to exploit them in MIP solvers (pp. 22, 28, 34, 37-39).

method_links.note: Journal version: matrix-based detector with numeric fit and no-op path; tuning aimed not to slow general MIPs; target, public general and broad CPLEX-internal numbers reported; nosep rows about 1.00; modeltype auto-detect; conservative defaults kept against class gains.

Gate evidence changed between versions: the report's SCIP-only study with the cut.set gain is replaced in the journal by general-MIP sets in both solvers, where releasing Ψmax deteriorates CPLEX; the SKILL's 'helped SCIP but not CPLEX' follows the report.

Partial: root gap closed, nodes and time side by side; nodes down/time up on fc, fctp called not paying; effort capped in solver units; cut counts beside time. Time split missing: speed inferred from nosep rows.
Incumbent cut families become special cases of one aggregation plus MIR; sweeps read per set with affected and cut counts; default set conservatively rather than at a knee.
Knock-out from full default, wins at ±10%, affected rows, conclusions refused on 16 and 3 affected public models and accepted on the large set; no seeds.
SKILL dates the bracket form from 2014, but this 2010 paper (and its 2009 report) already reads the CPLEX-internal set in >=10 s and >=100 s subsets by the slower version, in a narrower form.
Disjoint test sets by stated rule, detector checked against known original structure before speed tests, same machine and version with caveat, per-instance data in companion report.
Network-design toolbox and embedded-network detection imported into a general MIP solver and mapped onto c-MIR; extra pieces tested and dropped; practitioner step only inferred from co-authorship.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: thin layer over the mature engine
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Compute only the new input (weights u and multipliers γ) and leave the cut machinery to the solver; R014 shows the same pattern.
Detection measured against the known original networks, with and without presolve, with the cause of each failure named.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: heuristic errors cost time, never validity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Cuts are MIR inequalities of aggregated original rows, so a wrong detection only makes cuts weak or dense; the gate trades speed alone.

transferable: [D1] Name the precise reason a general routine misses a known cut family (unknown structure, a cap on the aggregation length), and remove that reason (p. 3).
[D2] Implement structure-specific cuts as an aggregation heuristic for the existing c-MIR: compute the weights and multipliers only (pp. 3, 23).
[D4] Use a majority vote across commodities and keep the minority votes as an inconsistency ratio that gates the component (pp. 11, 20).
[D4] Shrink the network with slack-minus-|dual| weights to a few clusters, enumerate all cuts, and keep those with connected shores (pp. 25–26).
[D4] Find the most violated flow-cutset inequality in linear time by starting from δ−(S) and dropping the arcs with f*_a < r·y*_a (p. 25).

[D5] Validate a structure detector against ground truth before measuring speed: report detected and consistent counts, the maximum inconsistency, and the mean % deviation in nodes, arcs and commodities (pp. 21–22).
[D5] Report all, affected and unaffected rows per set, with ≥ 10 s and ≥ 100 s subsets defined by the slower run (pp. 29, 33–34).
[D5] Split easy and hard instances, and judge the hard part by gap measures (pp. 29, 31, 33).
[D7] Hedge exactly where the affected counts are small (pp. 34–35).

quotes.text: It is important to understand that our framework is not explicitly generating cutting planes. It only calculates weight vectors u.
In contrast to Table 3 and Scip we can trust these values since the overall testset is very large with a reasonable number of affected instances.

title: ParaSCIP - a parallel extension of SCIP
contribution: A distributed-memory parallel extension of SCIP that runs unmodified SCIP processes under a load coordinator with load balancing and checkpointing, and used up to 2048 cores of HLRN II to solve two previously open MIPLIB2003 instances, ds and stp3d (pp. 2, 5-12).
problem_entry: Two entries: branch-and-cut decisions depend on each other so dynamic load balancing is essential, and six MIPLIB2003 instances remained open since 2007; goal: a parallel SCIP on HLRN II solving two of them, scaling to >= 10,000 cores (pp. 3, 5).
key_idea: Parallelise at the subtree level with each SOLVER a full SCIP; a LOADCOORDINATOR presolves and broadcasts once, then sends bound changes; all novelty in the coordination layer (load balancing, checkpointing) (pp. 2, 5-9).
assumptions: General MIP (Definition 1); test instances ds (duty scheduling) and stp3d (Steiner tree packing); distributed memory without swap; correctness asserted: parameter changes affect only the path, not the result (pp. 4, 9-11).
experiments: SCIP 1.2.1.2 with CPLEX 12.1 on HLRN II MPP2, 512-2048 cores per job; proven optima 93.52 (ds, 17 jobs, ~86 h) and 493.71965 (stp3d, 11 jobs, ~114 h); idle ratios 2.2% and 3.9%; per-job tables; no baseline, speed-up curve, repeated runs or fixed settings (pp. 9-13).
positioning: Against earlier large-scale parallel MIP work (Xu et al., Ralphs et al.) that struggled to match sequential solvers; many open instances first solved sequentially; collecting mode similar to ParaLEX [17] (pp. 2-4, 7).
writing: Short report in workflow order, headline is the record, future-SCIP-progress argument in abstract and conclusion, candid about underestimated node counts (pp. 2, 5-12).
limits_future: Ramp-up/ramp-down time grows with cores, loss vs finer-grained parallelism unknown, other open instances remain; future: predict suitability for massive parallel solving and remaining run time (pp. 12-13).

method_links.note: Platform reuse taken to its limit: whole sequential SCIP is the parallel unit and inherits future progress; but the harness was not held fixed, settings changed between jobs and restarts leave statistics incomplete. Co-signed; second of five authors.
Run time split into ramp-up, solving and idle time and scaling limit located in ramp-up/ramp-down, but no payoff measure: effective-use claim rests on idle-time proxy with no speed-up or baseline.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: thin layer over the mature engine
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The unmodified SCIP is the parallel unit; ParaSCIP profits from future SCIP progress; compare D011 pp. 3, 23.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: heuristic errors cost time, never validity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Only asserted here: changed settings alter the solver's path, not the result; compare D011 p. 35.

transferable: [D2] Broadcast the presolved instance once, then send subproblems as bound-change lists relative to it (p. 6).

[D4] Keep at least p nodes within a relative dual-bound threshold in the coordinator's pool; when the pool runs low, switch selected solvers to best-bound or best-estimate collecting, and switch back once it holds more than mp·p (p. 7).
[D4] Let a solver whose subtree bound is poor compared with the pool's best bound request a new node and delay its current one (p. 8).
[D4] Checkpoint only primitive nodes, and on restart presolve them as subproblem roots; this also re-balances the hardest part of the tree (pp. 8–9).
[D4] Before a very long run, iterate aggressive presolving and strong-branching fixings on one machine until a fixpoint (p. 10).
[D5] Print one row per job of a checkpointed run, including unproductive jobs, together with the idle-time ratio (pp. 11–12).
coauthors: Yuji Shinano, Timo Berthold, Stefan Heinz, Thorsten Koch

quotes.text: This makes the parallelization development independent of the SCIP development. Thus, ParaSCIP directly profits from any algorithmic progress in future versions of SCIP.
These changes only influence the path the solver takes, not the overall result.
